text.summary: Sweet potato is a fast-spreading, frost-tender vine grown for its starchy roots, and its young leaves and shoots are eaten too. It is started from rooted shoots called slips rather than seed, and wants warm soil, plenty of sun and a long frost-free season. Compact bush types save space, and a large pot can work.
text.how_to_plant: Plant once frost has passed and the soil has warmed to about 18 degrees C. Start from slips, which are shoots sprouted from roots kept from an earlier crop; they are not sown like seed. Choose a sunny site with loose, well-drained soil. Plant each slip roughly 5 to 15 cm deep, depending on the guide, and water it in straight away. Space plants about 20 to 90 cm apart, with more room where the vines may roam, and set rows or ridges 75 to 180 cm apart. Where space is tight, try a compact bush type in a large pot.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist while the slips root and the plants settle in, since early drought does the most harm. Never leave the soil waterlogged, because that can rot roots. Go easy on fertiliser, especially nitrogen: rich soil grows leaves rather than roots, and a soil test shows what is needed. Vines grow fast, so give them room. Rotate beds to reduce nematodes and scurf, and avoid ground that was lawn or overgrown with perennial grass the year before, to reduce wireworm.
text.harvest: Expect roughly 85 to 150 days from planting, depending on variety and warmth. Dig when the leaves start to yellow or the vine tops die back, and before frost. Roots keep growing, so start checking their size from about 80 days. Cure freshly dug roots before storing them, to heal wounds and sweeten them. Then store them cool, dark and ventilated, never in the fridge and never colder than about 10 degrees C. Cured roots can last several months. Young leaves and shoots are edible too.
common_mistakes: Planting slips into cold soil or before frost has passed.
Feeding generously, especially with nitrogen, which gives leafy vines and few roots.
Letting newly planted slips dry out before they root.
Refrigerating roots or storing them below about 10 degrees C.
Storing roots without curing them first.

text.summary: Lettuce is a fast-growing, upright annual leaf crop that prefers cool weather and tolerates light frost. In heat it turns bitter and runs to seed, so shade, steady moisture and slow-bolting varieties help. It grows in beds and in containers, and leaf types can be picked a few leaves at a time.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny site with loamy soil at a pH of about 6.0 to 6.7. Sow seed very shallowly: pressed onto the surface or covered lightly, never deeper than about 2.5 cm. It usually comes up within one to two weeks, best in cool soil and poorly in hot soil, so do not sow when the ground is hot. You can also raise transplants indoors or buy them; head types in particular suit bought transplants. Space leaf types about 10 to 25 cm apart and heading types 25 to 38 cm, with rows 30 to 90 cm apart. Sow again every 10 to 14 days for a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Water frequently enough to keep the soil evenly moist. Dry soil can push plants to bolt, but soggy soil invites rots. Mulch lightly to hold moisture. In hot weather give afternoon shade or shade cloth, and favour slow-bolting loose-leaf types over heading ones. Light frost is tolerated, but cover plants with a frost blanket in colder weather. A general feed can go in at planting, with one extra dose of nitrogen while the plants grow; follow the label.
text.harvest: Allow about 50 to 80 days from sowing, leaf types being quicker. Leaf types can be picked as baby leaves about 5 to 8 cm long or when plants reach about 13 to 15 cm tall. Take the outer leaves first and leave the centre growing, or cut the whole plant at ground level. Heading types are cut once, as a whole head. Harvest before a flower stalk forms, because bolted leaves turn bitter. Store in the fridge: crisphead keeps about two to three weeks, while leaf and butterhead types keep roughly one to two weeks, and up to four if bagged dry.
common_mistakes: Sowing into hot soil, where seed germinates poorly.
Letting the soil dry out or swing between wet and dry, which pushes plants to bolt and can cause tipburn.
Overwatering or poor drainage, which encourages rots and leaf disease.
Growing heading types through hot weather instead of loose-leaf or slow-bolting ones.
Planting seed too deeply; this tiny seed needs only a light cover or none.

text.summary: Mint, here spearmint, is a vigorous perennial herb grown for its leaves. It spreads fast by underground runners, so most guides advise a container or a confined bed. It copes with sun or part shade, likes evenly moist soil, and is sensitive to frost. Cuttings and divisions are the easiest way to get new plants.
text.how_to_plant: Most gardeners start mint from a rooted cutting, a division of an established clump, or a bought plant, because seedlings grown from seed often differ from the parent. Seed needs only a very shallow covering and sprouts in 10 to 14 days. Choose sun or part shade and well-drained soil. Space plants roughly 30 to 45 cm apart. Grow them in a pot of at least 10 litres, or in a bed with the roots confined, so they cannot spread through the garden.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, because too much water encourages root and leaf diseases. Water early in the day, or use drip irrigation, so leaves are not wet overnight, which invites rust. Pinch shoot tips and cut back often to keep growth bushy, and remove flower spikes to hold the leaf flavour. Divide crowded plants every three to four years. Watch for runners creeping over the pot rim and trim them. At the end of the season, cutting plants right back discourages pests and disease.
text.harvest: Start picking once plants stand about 8 to 10 cm tall, taking leaves or leafy stem tips whenever you need them. Frequent cutting encourages bushy new growth. Leaves taste strongest just before the plant flowers, which is the best time to cut for drying. Fresh mint keeps about a week in the fridge with the stems in water. Dry stems in a shaded, airy place, or freeze chopped leaves in water in an ice cube tray.
common_mistakes: Planting it loose in a bed, where it spreads and crowds out other plants.
Overwatering or leaving the soil soggy, which invites root and leaf disease.
Leaving the leaves wet overnight, which favours rust.
Letting plants flower, which dulls the leaf flavour.
Expecting seed-grown plants to match the parent; mints hybridise, so use cuttings or divisions to keep a type.

text.summary: Sweet basil is a tender annual herb grown for its fragrant leaves. It needs warm soil and sun, is damaged by frost, and does well in beds and in pots. Pinching out the tips makes plants branch.
text.how_to_plant: Wait until frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, about 16 C or more; nights should stay above about 10 C. Pick a sunny spot with well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Sow seed only 3 to 6 mm deep; it usually sprouts in about 5 to 10 days, sometimes up to two weeks. Seed can also be started indoors three to six weeks before planting out. Space plants roughly 25 to 60 cm apart, with rows 45 to 90 cm apart. Compact types are well suited to pots.
text.how_to_care: Water at the base, with drip or by hand, so the leaves stay dry. This lowers the risk of downy mildew, as do sun, airflow and uncrowded plants. Pinch growing tips to make plants branch, and remove flower buds as they appear. Go easy on nitrogen feed, which can affect flavour. In hot spells a little afternoon shade helps. Protect plants on cold nights, since leaves blacken in the cold.
text.harvest: Start picking once a plant has six to eight leaves. Cut stems with clean scissors, leaving a few leaves on each stem, or pinch off tips or single leaves, and never strip more than a third of the plant at one time. Flavour is strongest when flower buds have formed but not opened. Removing tips makes plants branch. Fresh sprigs do not keep well, and sources disagree about the fridge. Drying or freezing keeps the surplus.
common_mistakes: Planting out too early, while frost or cold nights can still blacken the leaves.
Watering over the leaves or crowding plants, which favours downy mildew.
Letting flower buds open instead of pinching them off, which takes energy from leaf growth.
Heavy nitrogen feeding, which one source says affects flavour.
Cutting more than a third of the plant at once, which can stop it producing.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant sends up a flower stalk and heads for seed instead of making more leaves.
prevention: Do not sow so early that young plants meet cold spells
Pinch out flower stalks as soon as they show, to keep the leaves coming

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: A white, powdery coating forms on the leaves, which can distort and drop early.
prevention: Do not overplant, so air can move between the plants
Space plants out
Avoid watering over the leaves
Remove and dispose of badly affected plant parts

problems.name: Root rot
problems.signs: In excessively wet soil the roots lack air and begin to rot.
prevention: Avoid overwatering
Keep drainage around the plants good
Remove affected plants and improve drainage for the others

prevention: Knock aphids off the plants with a strong spray of water

text.summary: Parsley is a leafy herb grown for its fresh leaves and usually treated as an annual, though it is really a biennial. Curled and flat-leaf types both suit full sun or part shade, fertile well-drained soil and a steady supply of moisture. The seed is slow to sprout, so patience at the start pays off.
text.how_to_plant: Soak the seed overnight to help it germinate, because parsley is slow to sprout. Sow it 5 to 12 mm deep, either where it will grow or in trays about nine weeks before planting out, and expect seedlings in two to four weeks. Choose fertile, well-drained soil in full sun or part shade. Thin the seedlings to roughly 15 to 40 cm apart, in rows 30 to 45 cm apart. Handle seedlings gently, since the taproot dislikes being disturbed. In a pot, use quality potting mix and a container of at least 40 litres.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, as waterlogged ground can rot the roots. A layer of straw mulch helps hold moisture. A balanced fertiliser suits it. Leave room between plants so air can move and mildew is less likely. Pinch out flower stalks as soon as they show, to keep leaves coming. The plant is hardy in the cold, but long spells above about 32 degrees Celsius slow growth sharply, so give some afternoon shade in hot climates. It can also be grown indoors.
text.harvest: Snip stems and leaves as you need them, taking no more than a third of the plant at once so it keeps growing. Stems are ready when they carry about three leaf segments and the leaves are dark green. For a larger amount, cut the whole plant. Fresh sprigs stay good standing in a container of water out of direct sun, or wrapped in a bag in the refrigerator. Leaves can also be dried and kept in an airtight container. Handling the plant and then standing in strong sun can irritate skin.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil stay waterlogged, which can rot the roots.
Planting too thickly, which cuts airflow and invites mildew.
Leaving flower stalks on the plant, which shortens the harvest.
Sowing too early in cold weather, which can push first-year plants to flower.
Moving seedlings roughly, when the taproot should be disturbed as little as possible.

problems.name: Mexican bean beetle
problems.signs: Rounded coppery or tan beetles marked with black spots, plus yellow egg clusters under the leaves. Their larvae chew leaves and pods and harm small plants most.
prevention: Pick off beetles, larvae and egg clusters by hand
Cover early plantings with floating row cover to keep beetles off
Clear crop residue after harvest to stop numbers building up

problems.name: Aphids and mites
problems.signs: Leaves wilt, dry out or become discoloured where these pests feed. Aphids can also spread bean mosaic virus.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water
Encourage predatory insects

problems.name: Seed rot, root rot and damping off
problems.signs: Seeds rot in cold soil. Seedlings darken, wilt and die, usually in cool, wet conditions.
prevention: Sow only once the soil is warm
Let the soil dry between waterings
Keep the soil well drained
Rotate crops

problems.name: Bean blight
problems.signs: Small water-soaked spots that grow into large patches on stems, leaves and pods.
prevention: Water carefully and let the soil dry between waterings

problems.name: Bean mosaic virus
problems.signs: Yellow blotches and distorted leaves.
prevention: Choose varieties resistant to bean common mosaic virus
Keep aphids down, as they spread it
Pull out affected plants

problems.name: Blossom drop
problems.signs: Flowers fall without setting pods during hot or dry spells; pods usually set again as days cool.
prevention: Keep soil moisture even while plants flower

text.summary: Green or snap bean is a frost-tender annual grown for its young, tender pods. It comes as low bush types and taller climbing pole types, and it is sown straight into warm soil where it will grow. Both like full sun and well-drained soil, and the pods are picked while still young.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed directly in the garden once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to at least about 15.6 degrees C; seed germinates in roughly 6 to 15 days. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil. Sow about 0.6 to 5 cm deep, with plants roughly 5 to 30 cm apart in rows about 30 to 100 cm apart. Climbing types need a trellis, tripod or stakes; bush types usually stand alone. Transplants are not recommended, because the roots dislike disturbance. Sow again every 1.4 to 3 weeks for a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Water with most care while plants flower and set pods. Avoid waterlogged soil, which invites root rot, and avoid splashing the leaves. Mulch around the plants to hold moisture and hold back weeds. Heavy nitrogen feeding delays flowering and cuts pod set, so go easy. Hot spells above about 32 degrees C can make blossoms drop. Pick pods often to keep plants producing.
text.harvest: Pick snap beans while the pods are young, firm and tender, before the seeds swell enough to bulge or show through. A ready pod snaps cleanly when bent. Guides give about 50 to 110 days from sowing to the first picking, and the harvest runs for roughly 2 to 6 weeks, longer on climbing types. Picking often keeps plants cropping, while pods left to mature slow later production. Fresh pods keep in the fridge for about a week and can be frozen for longer.
common_mistakes: Sowing before frost has passed or into cold soil, where seed rots or germinates poorly.
Letting pods grow too large before picking, so they turn tough and the seeds bulge.
Overwatering or leaving the soil waterlogged, which encourages root rot.
Feeding too much nitrogen, which delays flowering and reduces pod set.
Transplanting seedlings, because beans dislike root disturbance.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White, powdery patches show on the older leaves and spread upwards, and in bad cases cover the whole plant.
prevention: Water early in the day so the leaves dry before evening
Avoid overcrowding and stake tall types so air moves through the plants
Mulch to keep spores from splashing up from the soil
Grow early-maturing or resistant varieties

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Green to pinkish insects cluster on the underside of leaves near new growth.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water
Grow virus-resistant varieties
Avoid over-feeding, which increases their numbers

problems.name: Pea weevil
problems.signs: A small brownish or greyish beetle with light markings on its back. Its larvae feed inside the peas and leave circular chambers, with an opaque window visible on dry seed.
prevention: Start from clean, uninfested seed, which is the main way the pest spreads
Sow and pick early, which reduces exposure

problems.name: Black spot and foot rot
problems.signs: Small purple spots form on the leaves and may enlarge and blacken, and affected leaves often die. Stems, flowers and pods can be spotted, and young plants may die from damage at the soil line.
prevention: Grow in well-drained soil in a sunny spot
Support the plants on a trellis
Use clean seed
Remove and destroy infected crop remains
Avoid planting peas in the same spot the following season

problems.name: Fusarium wilt
problems.signs: Plants yellow from the bottom upwards, wilt and may be stunted, and leaves curl downward while stems turn brittle. Inside the root and lower stem the tissue is discoloured, brick red in one guide and yellow-orange in another.
prevention: Start from healthy seed
Keep peas out of the same bed for as long as you can
Grow resistant varieties and sow early, so the crop develops before the soil warms up

problems.name: Seed rot and root rot
problems.signs: Seeds rot in cold soil, and seedlings are stunted with yellowing lower leaves.
prevention: Improve soil drainage
Avoid compacted or wet soil

text.summary: Pea is a cool-season annual grown for its seeds, or for the whole pod in snow and snap types. It likes full sun and well-drained soil, tolerates light frost and is sown straight into the garden. Tall types climb a trellis, while dwarf types stay low. Hot weather makes the flowers drop.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where it will grow, in a sunny spot with well-drained soil, once the soil has reached 4.4 degrees C. Seed sprouts in roughly 7 to 35 days, slowest in cold soil. Sow about 1.3 to 5 cm deep and 2.5 to 20 cm apart in the row, with rows from 20 cm to well over a metre apart, wider where a trellis will stand. Put the trellis up at sowing for tall types. Transplants are usually not advised. Sow again every 2 to 5 weeks to spread the harvest.
text.how_to_care: Hold moisture steady, with no heavy soaking while the plants are in flower, and water at the base or early in the day so the leaves dry before evening. Mulch to save moisture and hold back weeds. Go easy on nitrogen, which pushes leaf growth at the cost of pods. Tall types need a trellis, a cage or a fence, while dwarf types may manage alone. Hot spells above about 27 degrees C can make flowers fall. Leave one to four years before peas return to the same bed.
text.harvest: Pick shelling peas when the pods are plump and full but still crisp, before the seeds turn starchy. Snow peas are picked while the pods are flat and the seeds tiny, and snap peas once the pods have sized up; check these every day or two. Guides give roughly 50 to 112 days from sowing to the first picking, with cropping that runs for about 3 to 10 weeks. Fresh pods keep in the fridge, and shelled peas freeze well.
common_mistakes: Letting plants flower in hot weather, when the flowers drop and pods fail to set; sow early so pods form while it is still cool.
Feeding too much nitrogen, which gives lush leaves but poor flowering and few pods.
Picking snow and snap peas late, after the pods have gone fibrous.
Soaking the plants heavily while they flower, which can interfere with pollination.
Crowding plants or wetting the leaves late in the day, which helps powdery mildew.

text.summary: Radish is a root crop sown straight into the ground. It likes a sunny spot with loose, well-drained soil and little feeding, and it also suits containers. Roots are ready roughly 20 to 60 days after sowing, and repeat sowings every week or two keep them coming. Avoid hot weather and swings between wet and dry soil.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground where the plants will grow. Seed can go in once the soil reaches about 4 degrees C, and it comes up best between roughly 7 and 30 degrees C, usually within 3 to 14 days. Sow about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep, in rows 20 to 61 cm apart, and thin the seedlings; guides give final gaps from a few centimetres up to about 20 cm. Pick a sunny spot with loose, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil, rich in organic matter, at a pH of about 6 to 6.8. Radishes also grow well in containers. Sow a little more seed every week or two for a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist: swings between dry and wet split the roots, and slow growth makes them woody and hot-tasting. Radishes need little feeding, and extra nitrogen grows leaves at the expense of roots. Mulch around the plants to hold moisture. A floating row cover keeps flea beetles and root maggots off, netting keeps caterpillars away, and a collar around each seedling stops cutworms. Grow radishes in a different spot each year. Hot weather pushes plants to flower and makes roots woody, so avoid sowing in very hot weather.
text.harvest: Pull the whole plant while the roots are still small, about 2.5 cm across or less, then trim off the tops. Expect the first roots roughly 20 to 60 days after sowing, depending on the type and the weather. Left too long, roots turn pithy, woody and hot-tasting, and they may crack. Refrigerate them in a bag; guides give anywhere from about 5 days to 4 weeks. The leaves and young seed pods can be eaten too.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil swing between dry and wet, which cracks and splits the roots.
Leaving radishes in the ground too long, so the roots turn pithy, hot and woody.
Sowing in hot weather, which brings flower stalks and woody roots.
Feeding with too much nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of roots.
Sowing too thickly and not thinning, which gives small roots.

text.summary: Rosemary is an evergreen, fragrant herb that grows as a perennial shrub. It wants full sun and light, well-drained soil, copes with dry spells once settled, and does well in pots or in the ground. It is best started from cuttings, as seed is slow and unreliable.
text.how_to_plant: Start from a rooted cutting, which succeeds more often than seed. Seed is slow and uneven, usually sprouting within two to four weeks if you do try it. Pick a spot with at least six hours of sun and light, sandy or loamy, well-drained soil with a pH of about 6 to 7. A raised or slightly mounded bed drains best. Sources suggest anywhere from 20 to 150 centimetres between plants. In a pot, give each plant at least 20 litres.
text.how_to_care: Rosemary is easy to overwater, so allow the soil to dry between waterings and never leave a pot standing in water. Once established it copes well with dry spells. It seldom needs feeding, and too much fertiliser cuts flowering and fragrance. Prune after flowering to keep it neat, and pinch the tips of young plants to shape them. Leave space between plants so air can move and mildew stays away. A healthy plant tolerates a light freeze; where winters are harsher, grow it in a pot and bring it to a sunny indoor spot before the first frost.
text.harvest: Cut sprigs or leafy tips as you need them once the plant has grown large enough, taking no more than about a fifth of the growth at a time and letting it recover between pickings. Use the leaves fresh, keep cut stems in the fridge, hang bundles to dry, or slice and freeze them. Dried leaves keep well in an airtight container.
common_mistakes: Overwatering, which is the biggest cause of decline and death.
Planting in wet, poorly drained clay soil.
Crowding plants so air cannot move between them, which invites powdery mildew.
Counting on seed, which germinates slowly, unevenly and often poorly.
Over-fertilising, which reduces flowering and fragrance.

text.summary: Tomato is a warm-season fruiting vegetable that needs plenty of sun and frost-free weather. Bush types stay compact and ripen most fruit together, while vine types keep growing and need support. Small types suit large pots. Even watering protects the fruit, and very hot nights can stop large types from setting it.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil rich in organic matter, at a pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Sow seed 5 to 8 mm deep. Sow where it will grow only in warm regions, where soil and nights stay warm; otherwise raise seedlings in pots first. Plant out only once frost danger has passed. Set each plant deeper than it sat in its pot, so only the top few leaf sets show. Allow 30 to 120 cm between plants, closer for dwarf types and wider for vigorous or caged vines, and at least 60 cm between rows. Avoid soil where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant or potatoes grew in the last three years.
text.how_to_care: Water thoroughly and evenly, and avoid swings between drought and soaking. Uneven watering causes cracked fruit and blossom end rot, so spread a mulch of straw, chopped leaves or compost to hold moisture. Support vine types with stakes, cages or a trellis; bush types also do best staked or caged. On staked plants, remove side shoots so only a few main stems remain. Begin feeding when you plant out, then keep topping up during the growing season as the product label directs.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit roughly 55 to 90 days after planting out, depending on the variety. Start picking as soon as colour begins to change; this cuts cracking, splitting and insect damage and gives more usable fruit. You can instead leave fruit on the vine until fully coloured but still firm, which gives the best flavour. Vine types keep cropping until the first frost, while bush types give most of their crop in one burst, so plan for a glut.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost danger has passed, which injures the top growth.
Watering unevenly, which brings blossom end rot and split fruit.
Planting shallow instead of burying the stem so only a few leaf sets show.
Growing tomatoes again in soil that held tomatoes, peppers, eggplant or potatoes within three years.

text.summary: Eggplant is a warm-season fruiting vegetable that wants full sun, fertile well-drained soil and a long stretch of warm weather. It is tender to frost and sets fruit poorly when nights are cool. Most gardeners start with transplants. Small and dwarf types suit pots, and most plants need a stake or cage.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil, ideally sandy loam enriched with compost, at about pH 5.5 to 7.2. Germinate seed indoors at a soil temperature near 21 to 32 C, covering it with only about half a centimetre of mix, then grow the seedlings on for 6 to 10 weeks in all. Seedlings usually show in one to two weeks. Plant out only when frost danger has passed and the soil and nights are warm, since cool conditions stunt the plants. Space plants about 46 to 91 cm apart in rows 60 to 120 cm apart, and set a stake or cage in at planting. In pots, pick a large one and a compact type.
text.how_to_care: Water steadily and deeply rather than often, and keep the soil moist through flowering and fruit development, because dry spells then cut flowering and fruit set. A drip line or soaker keeps the leaves dry. Once the soil is warm, mulch to hold moisture. Set plants against their support as they grow, and pinch out the growing tip when young plants are about 30 cm tall so they branch. Give a starter feed at planting and a second feed once fruit appears, following the product label. Rotate crops to limit wilt.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit about 50 to 80 days after planting out, depending on the variety; plants grown from seed all the way take longer. Pick while the skin is glossy and the fruit is firm, before it dulls or yellows. For the usual large type that is roughly 15 to 20 cm long. Cut the stem with pruners or a knife, and wear gloves because the stem can be spiny. Picking often encourages more fruit.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost has passed or while the soil is still cold, which kills or stunts young plants.
Watering little and often instead of soaking deeply, which keeps roots shallow.
Leaving fruit on until the skin turns dull or yellow.
Laying organic mulch on cold soil before it has warmed.

text.summary: Potato is grown from seed potatoes, which are tubers, not from seed. It wants full sun, well-drained soil and a few months to crop, and frost can harm it. Soil is drawn up around the stems as the plants grow, so the new tubers stay covered and do not turn green.
text.how_to_plant: Start with certified disease-free seed potatoes rather than tubers saved from your own crop. Cut large tubers so each piece keeps at least one eye, and let the cut surfaces dry. Plant once the soil has warmed to about 15 C, 2.5 to 15 cm deep and roughly 13 to 51 cm apart, in rows at least 50 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil. Whole tubers hold up better than cut pieces in hot soil. A large pot about 50 cm deep, with good drainage holes, can also work.
text.how_to_care: Draw soil up around the stems as they grow, so light cannot reach the tubers and turn them green and bitter. A thick straw mulch helps keep the soil cool and moist. Potatoes are hungry plants, but too much fertiliser grows leaves at the expense of tubers. Keep water off the leaves, which can spread fungal disease. Pick off beetles by hand. Keep potatoes, tomatoes and other family members out of the same bed for three to four years.
text.harvest: Full-size potatoes are usually ready about 80 to 120 days after planting, once the foliage has yellowed and died back. If you plan to store them, leave the tubers in the ground for a couple of weeks after the tops die, then dig gently with a fork when the soil is dry, taking care not to skin them. Cure them for two to three weeks, then keep them in a cool, dark place. Cut away small green patches and discard very green tubers.
common_mistakes: Saving your own tubers as seed potatoes, which builds up viruses and diseases.
Leaving tubers exposed to light, which turns them green and bitter.
Planting cut pieces into hot soil, where they decay more readily than whole tubers.
Fertilising heavily, which grows leaves rather than tubers.
Digging the crop while the soil is wet.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant sends up a flower stalk and goes to seed early; leaf picking then ends. It happens as days lengthen and the weather warms.
prevention: Sow early enough that the crop grows while days are short and cool
Choose slow-bolting varieties for crops that will mature in warmer weather
Water regularly and deeply in hot weather to avoid heat stress

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.signs: Yellow to grey-brown patches on the leaves, especially on the undersides; worst in wet or humid seasons.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties
Water at soil level, not on the leaves
Remove and destroy affected leaves
Do not overcrowd plants, so air can flow between them

problems.name: Leaf miner
problems.signs: Maggots tunnel inside the leaf, leaving obvious winding trails as they feed.
prevention: Once seedlings are thinned, protect them under floating row covers

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.signs: Tender leaves and shoots are eaten, mostly at night, leaving slimy trails.
prevention: Remove their hiding places
Collect them by torchlight or trap them

problems.name: Damping off
problems.signs: Seeds seem not to germinate, or young plants rot as they come out of the soil.
prevention: Use new potting mix if raising seedlings
Do not water the foliage
Avoid waterlogged soil

text.summary: Spinach is a frost-hardy leaf crop that forms a low rosette of dark green leaves, about 20 to 30 cm tall. It bolts, running up flower stalks, as days lengthen and temperatures rise. Sow it where it will grow in fertile, well-drained soil, keep it moist and pick the leaves while they are young.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground or a roomy pot, 0.8 to 1.3 cm deep, in fertile, well-drained soil that holds plenty of organic matter. Wait until the soil is at least about 7.2 degrees C, and use seed packed for the current year. Seedlings usually show in 5 to 10 days. Thin them once they stand about 2.5 cm tall, leaving plants roughly 5 to 35 cm apart. Rows can sit 30 to 91 cm apart. Sow again about every 2 weeks to keep leaves coming. A pot needs at least 20 litres.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, watering deeply and regularly, because spinach grows best with plenty of water. It is a hungry crop, so dig in compost or fertiliser before sowing and feed again partway through the crop. Mulch holds moisture, keeps leaves clean and holds back weeds. Established plants shrug off frost. When days lengthen and the weather warms, plants send up flower stalks, so slow-bolting varieties are the better choice for warmer-weather crops. Give plants room, water at soil level and remove spotted leaves to limit downy mildew, and use row covers against leaf miners.
text.harvest: Pick individual leaves once a plant has about six true leaves, choosing tender dark green ones roughly 8 to 15 cm long. Cutting full-size leaves lets new ones grow from the centre. You can also cut whole plants at soil level, and late thinnings can be eaten. One guide gives about 28 to 55 days from sowing to a first picking. Once flower stalks appear, harvest what remains of the crop. Keep the leaves in a bag in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Growing the crop into warm weather and long days, which makes it bolt.
Letting the soil dry out; spinach wants steady moisture.
Leaving plants to run to seed instead of taking the rest of the crop once flower stalks form.
Crowding plants, which cuts air flow and invites downy mildew.
Sowing old seed, which loses viability quickly.

text.summary: Yardlong bean, also called snake bean or asparagus bean, is an annual climbing vine grown for its very long pods. It needs a strong trellis, a sunny spot and free-draining soil. Insects pollinate the flowers, and the young pods are picked often while the seeds inside are still small.
text.how_to_plant: Put up a strong, tall trellis first, because the vines can reach about 2 to 3.7 metres. Sow seed in the spot where it will grow, about 2.5 to 5 cm deep, with vines roughly 30 cm apart along the support. Choose a sunny site with free-draining loam or clay and a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.5, and make a raised bed if drainage is poor. Seedlings usually appear in about 6 to 14 days. Seedlings raised elsewhere can be set out once they have two true leaves.
text.how_to_care: Keep the vines on a sturdy trellis. Avoid soggy ground and frost, since both hold growth back and wet roots can rot. The crop copes with drought, but very humid weather can bring powdery mildew. Thin crowded vines so air moves through them, keep water off the leaves and cut away leaves that are badly infected. Do not overfeed once plants are growing. Bees and other insects pollinate the flowers. Yellowing, wilting plants in wet soil point to root rot, so improve drainage.
text.harvest: From sowing, first pods are ready after roughly 40 to 90 days, depending on location. Pick the pods young, while the seeds inside are still immature, when they are about 25 to 30 cm long; young pods are the most tender. Pick by hand often, even daily. For dried beans, leave some pods on the vine until the seeds are fully developed and mature.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil stay waterlogged, which slows growth and can rot roots.
Growing it where frost can reach it.
Skipping a strong, tall trellis.
Over-fertilising once plants are growing.
Leaving pods until the seeds are fully mature when tender pods are wanted.

Rule 87d: IPNI (s8) prints Leguminosae for this species; Fabaceae is the -aceae form, reached through Wikidata's parent-taxon chain (s16).

s3: a three year crop rotation is suggested to reduce potential disease and insect problems (rule 59). One source. s5 says disease can stay in the soil for several years and to grow cowpeas in a different area each year (no figure, rule 85c).

fields.value: For fresh shelling, pick when the seeds have reached full size and the pods shell easily, before the pods dry. For dry peas, leave the pods until they are tan, dry and brittle and the seeds are hard.
fields.note: s1 pods easily shelled, seeds swelling before pods lighten; s2 pea at full size; s4 seeds full size and firm before drying down; s5 seeds mature when pods turn tan, left to dry until brittle and seeds too hard to dent with a fingernail.

s2: store unshelled fresh pods in the refrigerator for about a week or more (fridge); shelled peas can be frozen after blanching ([paraphrase], freeze); dried shelled peas keep in a dry, cool place for many months (dry). One source each, s5 also says to store dry cowpeas in a cool, dark, dry, airtight container.

Cowpea, southern pea, black-eyed pea, bean, pea, Vigna and legume are absent from the UGA C1245 toxic lists (s12, not a complete list; only entry with 'bean' is Castor Bean, Ricinus communis, a different plant) and from the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s13, not all inclusive; only 'Castor Beans'). Cowpea, southern pea, black-eyed pea, bean, pea, Vigna, legume are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s10, 35 entries; only Castor Bean) and from both lists of the Utah brochure (s11). The brochure's toxic list has 'Sweet Pea'; that means Lathyrus odoratus, not this crop, so it does not count (rule 38). Castor Bean is Ricinus communis. That cowpeas are grown as food is not a toxicity finding.

problems.name: Seed rot and damping off in cold wet soil
problems.signs: Seed rots in the ground and young seedlings collapse after cold, wet weather at or just after sowing.
prevention: Sow only after the soil has warmed
Avoid waterlogged soil

problems.name: Fusarium wilt
problems.signs: Foliage yellows widely, few pods form and the plant can eventually die.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties

problems.name: Cowpea curculio
problems.signs: A small black weevil feeds on developing pods and lays eggs in the developing seeds.

problems.name: Frost injury
problems.signs: Frost damages pods and plant tissue.
prevention: Wait until all frost danger has passed before sowing

problems.name: Too much nitrogen
problems.signs: Plants make plenty of top growth, flower late and set fewer pods.
prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen
Side-dressing is usually not necessary

text.summary: Southern pea, also called cowpea or black-eyed pea, is a frost-tender annual grown from seed sown straight into warm soil. It likes full sun, copes well with dry spells and has a low feeding need. Plants come as bush or vining types, and the peas are picked fresh for shelling or left to dry.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the plants will grow, once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to at least 18.3 degrees C; cold, wet ground can rot seed. Place seeds about 1.3 to 5.1 cm deep and roughly 5.1 to 7.6 cm apart, in rows 51 to 122 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with well-draining loam or light clay, and avoid waterlogged ground. Guides accept a soil pH from about 5.5 to 7.5. Expect seedlings within about 4 to 14 days. One guide thins to about 30 cm. Sow again every 3 weeks for a steady supply of fresh peas.
text.how_to_care: Cowpeas tolerate dry spells, so water mainly around flowering and pod fill, and keep the soil from becoming waterlogged. Spread organic mulch to hold moisture. The crop has a low feeding need, and too much nitrogen gives leafy growth at the expense of pods. The flowers pollinate themselves. Rotate so the crop returns to the same soil only after about three years, to limit disease. Watering at the base of the plants suits hot, dry weather while they are in flower and podding.
text.harvest: From sowing, guides give a first harvest anywhere from about 50 to 125 days, depending on type. For fresh shelling, pick once the seeds have filled out and the pods open easily, before the pods start to dry. For dry peas, wait until the pods are tan, dry and brittle. Fresh pods keep in the fridge; shelled peas can be frozen after blanching, and fully dried peas store in a cool, dry place.
common_mistakes: Sowing into cold, wet soil, which rots seed and kills seedlings.
Planting before frost danger has passed.
Feeding with too much nitrogen, which grows leaves rather than pods.
Letting the soil become waterlogged.
Leaving fresh pods on the plant until they begin to dry when shelling peas are wanted.

fields.note: s2 and s8 name su, se and sh2 types; s1 says the sh2 gene needs isolation from standard sweet corn and gives a warmer sowing temperature for extra-sweet types; s3 says early maturing cultivars tend to produce relatively small plants and names three basic hybrid types.

s1 'requires full sun'; s2 'prefers full sun'; s4 quick-facts 'Full sun with protection from strong winds' (differs from the Yates tomato page, so not template). s8 repeats s2 (same group). Not counted: s3's sun line (word for word on the Maryland tomato page, template); s6's full-sun sentence names the variety True Gold; s7 says 'plenty of sunlight' (no hours).

Dissenting or lower figures (s2, s4, s8) are in this note, not in sources. 65 F = 18.3 C. Rule 88a: s1 gives a figure per type, 50 F = 10.0 C for standard types and 65 F for extra-sweet (super-sweet) types; the safer figure, the higher sowing temperature, is s1's figure, and it is not read as a range with 50 F. The stored 18.3 is therefore the extra-sweet or super-sweet figure of s1 and s3. s1: wait to plant extra-sweet types until the soil reaches 65 F; s3: super-sweet types should be planted when soil reaches 65 F (18.3 C); s2 and s8 (one group): above 60 F = 15.6 C for sowing seed; s4: sustained 16 C gives much better germination, practical germination minimum 12 C (the higher, 16, is s4's figure). Two independent sources state 18.3 (a figure given for one variety type counts as that source's figure, named here and flagged under rule 91b: both s1 and s3 give 65 F for the extra-sweet or super-sweet type). s1's 50 F is set aside under rule 88a and does not count toward the spread (rule 91g); s4's 12 C germination minimum is below its own 16 C sowing threshold, so 16 is s4's figure (rule 25). s4's 'if you wait until soil temperature has reached a sustained 16 C' is a sowing threshold (rule 91c). Remaining stated figures are 15.6 (s2, s8), 16 (s4) and 18.3 (s1, s3): spread 2.7 C, under 3 C, so no spread flag. Still flagged under rule 91b because the stored figure is for the sweeter types only. s7 says only 'after the soil warms'; no figure.

s3: 'Frost will injure top growth; needs warm weather to grow.' States that frost harms the crop, which is the 'tender' definition (harmed at 0 C). One source. The same Maryland slot reads 'Hardy annual' for spinach, so the line is set per crop (rule 83). s1, s2, s4, s7 give only planting cues (plant after frost danger is past), which do not count (rule 30). Flag: one source and an enum read from wording.

s2: 'Sweet corn will grow in all Utah soil types that are nutrient rich, well-drained, and fertile.' Under rule 91d, fertility and drainage qualifiers do not limit texture, so it states every texture. One source. No source dissents: s1 'most soil types' (rule 85d) and s7 'many soil types' name no excluded texture. s8 says only that sandy soils need watering more often and clayey soils less often.
s7: prefers well-drained soils with a pH between 5.5 and 7.0. ONE source; the other pages state no pH. Flag for the horticulturist.

s2 'prefers full sun and fertile, well-drained soil'; s4 quick-facts 'Rich, fertile and well-draining soil'; s7 'prefers well-drained soils'. s8 repeats s2 (same group). s6 says 'free-draining' (not the word 'well-drained'; not counted).

No source gives weeks, so weeks_indoors stays empty. s6's advice to sow in place is a one-variety page and is not counted (rule 88b).

Days to first harvest from sowing (page context, rule 33, except s5 which states it). Counted figures: s3 63 to 100 days (quick-facts line, no start point stated); s1 80 to 95 days after planting (seed in the ground); s4 75 to 100 days in warmer regions, 90 to 120 days in cooler areas, and 12 to 14 weeks = 84 to 98 days (quick-facts); s5 approximately 120 days from sowing. Not stored: s8 60 to 90 days (its sentence is s2's with 'from planting' removed; a page that copies another source's sentence adds no vote and no start point, rules 88d, 7 and 49, and s2 has no start point, rule 50). Corn, maize, Zea, sweet corn, corn plant, Dracaena and cornstalk are absent from the UGA C1245 toxic lists (s13, not a complete list; searched through the fetch tool) and from the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s14, read as text, not all inclusive; it names okra and cucumber only as plant defences). NC State Toolbox skipped (pending O-19). Absence is not evidence of safety.

Corn, maize, Zea and sweet corn are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s11, 35 entries) and from the toxic list of the Utah brochure (s12, read from the PDF). The brochure's non-toxic list has 'Corn Plant' and, as a separate entry, 'Dracaena'; the name 'Corn Plant' is shared (Wikidata lists 'corn plant' as an alias of maize, s10, and it is also a common name of a Dracaena houseplant), the entry does not name Zea mays, so it does not count (rule 38) and non_toxic is not used. That sweet corn is eaten is not a toxicity finding.

problems.name: Corn earworm
problems.signs: Caterpillars eat the silks and the ear tips: holes in the tips, silks gone and damp droppings near the silk.
prevention: Choose varieties whose husks close tightly over the ear tip
Remove the damaged part of the ear at harvest

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small green or black insects on leaves, tassels and ears. Heavily infested young plants crinkle and stunt, and sticky honeydew coats leaves and ears.
prevention: Dislodge them with a strong jet of water

problems.name: Poor kernel fill
problems.signs: Ears with gaps or poorly filled tips and few kernels, after drought or hot spells while tassels and silks are active.
prevention: Keep soil moist in dry weather
Plant at the spacing advised
Plant in a block of several rows rather than one long row
Keep feeding up so plants do not run short

problems.name: Corn smut
problems.signs: Swollen white fungal galls on the ears, stems or tassels.
prevention: Remove infected ears promptly from stalks and garden
Clear plant debris after harvest

problems.name: Cutworms
problems.signs: Young plants cut off close to the soil surface.
prevention: Place a small collar, such as a paper cup with the base cut out, around each seedling

problems.name: Seedling rot
problems.signs: Seedlings darken, wilt and die, usually in cool, wet soil.
prevention: Let the soil dry out before watering again

problems.name: Lodging
problems.signs: Plants fall over, for example in thunderstorms.
prevention: Run one or two strands of heavy string round the planting to hold stalks up

text.summary: Sweet corn is an annual grown for its ears of sweet kernels. It likes full sun, fertile well-drained soil and plenty of water, above all while the tassels open and the ears fill. Wind does the pollinating, so plant it in a block. Sweeter types are fussier about cold soil than standard types.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground once frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, about 18 degrees C or more; standard types tolerate slightly cooler soil than the sweeter types. Pick a sunny, well-drained, fertile spot out of strong wind. Place seeds about 2.5 to 5 cm deep and roughly 18 to 45 cm apart, with rows 60 to 90 cm apart, and plant several short rows side by side as a block. If two seeds go in each hole, thin to the stronger one. Sow again every 10 to 14 days for a longer supply. In a pot, use one at least 30 cm deep.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, taking most care while tassels open and ears fill, because dry spells then leave ears gappy. Corn is hungry, so work in a fertiliser before sowing and add a nitrogen side dressing partway through growth. Spread organic mulch round the base, away from young plants, to hold water and hold weeds back; weed gently so roots are not damaged. On a dry morning, a gentle shake of the plants as pollen sheds can help. Grow one type, or keep sweeter types apart, so cross-pollination does not spoil the sugar.
text.harvest: Expect the first ears roughly 63 to 120 days after sowing, depending on variety and temperature, and each sowing ripens over only about a week, so stagger sowings. Pick when the husk is still green, the silks have dried brown and a kernel squeezes out milky juice instead of watery juice. Eat quickly: sweetness fades with every day of storage, and fridge storage buys only a short time. Expect about one ear per plant, sometimes a smaller second.
common_mistakes: Sowing into cold soil, where seed germinates poorly.
Growing corn in one or two long rows, which gives poorly filled ears.
Letting plants run dry while tassels open and ears fill.
Planting sweeter types close to standard corn, which loses their extra sweetness.
Storing picked ears for days, which costs sweetness.
